A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same DIDS research. Their complete main texts, appendices, equations, tables, figures, and algorithm are readable and support reliable matching despite expanded supplementary material.

before.justification: v1 reports original nine-task evaluations, component ablations, computational costs, and sensitivity experiments in Tables 1–3 and Figures 2–3.

after.justification: v2 retains those original experiments and adds model/dataset evaluations, domain analyses, robustness tests, and unseen-task results in its appendices.

M1.justification: The gradient clustering, FIM-based impact calculation, loss forecasting, and sampling updates remain unchanged, including Algorithm 1. Appendix E discusses alternative divergences as possible extensions without establishing an implemented procedural change.

E1.justification: v2 adds OpenHermes-2.5 training data, HumanEval and MT-Bench evaluation in Appendix G, and unseen WMT16 English–German, TLDR, ARC-Challenge, and MBPP tasks in Appendix J. These substantially broaden coverage beyond the retained Tulu-3 and nine-task experiments.

E2.justification: The principal benchmark comparator set is retained. Table 10 adds fixed code/math-versus-general mixing strategies, while Table 12 extends the computational-cost comparison to DoReMi, DoGE, and Velocitune beyond the earlier DGA comparison. Newly cited DRPruning and DDK are not evaluated.

E3.justification: Added experiments introduce another reported 7B model configuration, a full 1,000k-sample OpenHermes control, static-mixture sweeps, swapping half of each domain's data, and unseen-task evaluation using BLEU, win rate, accuracy, and Pass@1. These are additional protocols; the original training hyperparameters and three-shot evaluation description remain.

E4.justification: Appendix D extends component ablations from four to all nine tasks and adds domain-weight trajectories, selection overlap, and clustering observations. Appendices G, H, and J add static-mixture sensitivity, corrupted-partition robustness, and generalization under diverse versus single-task guidance. Earlier sensitivity and irrelevant-data tests are retained.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, significance tests, or experimental error bars. The added tables continue the existing point-estimate reporting practice.

E6.justification: Tables 1–3 and the original plotted results are unchanged, including DIDS averages of 62.3 and 63.7. Tables 5–14 add extensive results, including a 63.7-to-60.2 decline under corrupted partitioning and a reported 53.5 average on unseen tasks. These concern newly reported conditions, not same-setting improvements over v1.

T1.justification: The original KL/FIM derivation and Johnson–Lindenstrauss material are retained. Appendix E adds a Cramér–Rao connection, properties asserted for the quadratic approximation, and a generalized metric-tensor expression for alternative divergences in Equation 19, without a new proof.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same three methodological contributions, 3.4% average-performance claim, comparable-efficiency claim, and emphasis on using approximately 10% of the training data. Additional appendix evidence supports these retained claims.

C2.justification: New appendix discussions explain performance through more decisive domain reweighting, interpret clustering by instructional format and shared reasoning patterns, and discuss specialization/general-data tradeoffs. They also interpret graceful degradation under corrupted partitions and cross-task transfer, including specialization effects on unrelated tasks. The original limitations section is unchanged.

D1.justification: v2 adds a code-access link, documents downstream-task adaptations of baselines, and supplies baseline proxy sizes, computational stages, and practical implementation guidance, including FIM batch sizes of 16–32. These are substantial documentation additions; they do not establish that unchanged benchmark results were rerun.

R1.justification: Section 2 adds DRPruning and DDK, distinguishing their pruning-recovery and knowledge-distillation settings from DIDS. Three introductory references, Li et al. (2023, 2024) and Wu et al. (2024), are removed. The central positioning against existing sampling strategies remains.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the main section order are preserved. Local edits clarify post-training terminology, standardize model names, revise author information, add acknowledgments, and expand related-work and baseline explanations. New appendix sections extend the supplement without extensively rewriting the original narrative.

P2.justification: v2 adds Tables 5–14 with model/dataset comparisons, expanded ablations, temporal domain weights, robustness, costs, and unseen-task results. Existing tables are regrouped and their captions moved below; Algorithm 1 becomes full-width and moves to the end. Figures 1–3 remain visually unchanged.

improvement.justification: v1's reported validation centers on one training dataset and tasks used to guide sampling. v2 substantially addresses this evidence gap through another training distribution, unseen-task evaluations under two guidance regimes, and corrupted-partition tests, supported by fuller ablations and reproducibility information. Reporting ambiguities temper these gains: Appendix B.3 claims shared gradient clustering despite Table 3's BERT-based DGA costing, and the added 'Mixtral-7B' name conflicts with its Mistral-7B footnote. Nevertheless, the broader tests substantially strengthen assessment of generalization and robustness.
